Merewillow Family Practice
24 September 2026
Dear Ms Brindle,
Re: Lena Orwick
I am writing at Ms Orwick’s request, with her consent, to summarise my assessment of her health.
On 9 September 2026 I examined Ms Orwick by telephone during a booked clinical consultation. We discussed
her sleep, mood and ability to manage ordinary activities, and I assessed her symptoms and mental state. She
was experiencing persistent anxiety, difficulty falling asleep and frequent waking. Her concentration had also
deteriorated, making routine tasks unusually demanding.
My assessment was of an anxiety condition with significant sleep disturbance. Taking the clinical history and
presentation together, my professional judgement is that this condition is consistent with the effects of domestic
abuse. This is my clinical opinion, rather than simply a record of an explanation offered by the patient.
We agreed a treatment plan and arranged a further appointment to review her sleep and anxiety. She has
remained engaged with her care despite finding conversations about her circumstances difficult.
I am a general practitioner registered with the General Medical Council and licensed to practise. My registration
and licence were current at the consultation and remain current at the date of this letter.
Yours sincerely,
Dr Amara Vennick
General Practitioner

notes: The letter records a patient message and administrative responses, but does not confirm a clinical examination or a professional judgement that an examined condition is consistent with domestic abuse. GP3 (missing): Receiving and reading a written patient message does not confirm an examination in person, by telephone or by video. GP4 (missing): The letter records the patient’s account but gives no clinician’s consistency judgement about injuries or a condition identified at examination. Basis: Schedule 1(11), guidance 2.52–2.60 and checklist, pp.18–21.

Alderfen Medical Rooms
Dr Cerys Halvern, General Practitioner
Registered with the General Medical Council; current licence to practise
18 August 2026
Dear Sir or Madam,
Re: Beatrice Nolling
Ms Nolling has asked for a letter recording the concerns she recently brought to the practice’s attention. She has
consented to the information below being shared with her solicitor.
On 12 August our reception team received a written message from Ms Nolling through the patient messaging
system. In it, she described feeling increasingly anxious, sleeping poorly and struggling to keep up with everyday
responsibilities. She also described restrictions on her access to household money and repeated demands to
account for where she had been.
I have read that message and understand why she wishes to obtain advice about her family circumstances. The
difficulties she describes deserve a sensitive response, particularly as she says that arranging private time to
speak can be challenging.
The practice has offered her a choice of appointment times and explained how she can ask for correspondence to
be handled discreetly. Her preferred arrangements for receiving letters have been noted on her record.
I hope this account of her communication with the practice is helpful. It records the information she supplied and
the practical steps we have taken in response.
Yours faithfully,
Dr Cerys Halvern
General Practitioner

Thistlemere Surgery
6 July 2026
Dear Mr Fenwick,
Re: Nadia Pelloran
Further to your request, and with Ms Pelloran’s permission, I have looked back at the entry concerning our
telephone contact on 25 June. This followed her request for a call about sleep difficulties and arrangements for
her next appointment.
During the call she mentioned recurrent nightmares, episodes of panic and difficulty concentrating at work. The
note also records that she was staying elsewhere following a period of intimidation and controlling behaviour
within her relationship. We discussed a quieter time for the practice to contact her and the availability of a
follow-up appointment.
In my professional judgement, the anxiety and disturbed sleep recorded on that occasion are consistent with a
condition arising in the context of domestic abuse. The symptoms were having a considerable effect on her
day-to-day functioning.
I have recomended that her next appointment allow sufficient time to discuss treatment options.
I am a GP with current General Medical Council registration and a licence to practise, both also held on 25 June.
Yours sincerely,
Dr Ivo Rennick
Dictated and signed

Brackenfold Health Practice
30 September 2026
Private correspondence
Re: Tomas Wetherell
Consultation
I examined Mr Wetherell by video on 22 September 2026. The appointment included a clinical history, visual
assessment of the affected areas and questions about pain and movement. The picture and sound were adequate
for that assessment.
Findings
There was visible bruising over his upper arm and mild swelling around one wrist. He described tenderness when
using that hand. Movement was preserved, although uncomfortable. I also identified marked anxiety and disrupted
sleep. We discussed care for the wrist and the circumstances in which he should seek an in-person review.
Clinical opinion
The findings, considered alongside the history obtained during the consultation, fit with injuries and anxiety
associated with domestic abuse. This is my medical assessment of his presentation; I cannot determine the
precise mechanism of each injury from a video consultation.
I provide this summary with Mr Wetherell’s consent. I am a general practitioner registered with the General
Medical Council and licensed to practise. I held that registration and licence when I examined him and continue to
hold both today.
Dr Elin Marrick
General Practitioner

Brackenmere Family Practice
24 September 2026
Dear Ms Fenwick,
Re: Tessa Marlow
You asked whether we could provide a medical account of Ms Marlow’s earlier attendance. With her written
consent, I have reviewed the consultation entry and subsequent treatment records held by this practice. I did not
conduct the original examination.
Ms Marlow was examined in person on 18 November 2022 by my colleague, Dr Elin Voss, a general practitioner
who was registered with the General Medical Council and licensed to practise at that time. Dr Voss remains
registered and licensed, but is currently on extended leave and unavailable to prepare this letter. I am also a
GMC-registered general practitioner with a licence to practise, held both at the time of that consultation and today.
The entry describes persistent disturbed sleep, heightened anxiety and difficulty concentrating. Dr Voss recorded
a clinical assessment of an anxiety condition, rather than simply reproducing the account Ms Marlow gave. Her
recorded professional judgement was that the condition and its presentation were consistent with Ms Marlow
having experienced domestic abuse within her former relationship. No physical injury was recorded at that
appointment.
The later notes show that sleep and day-to-day functioning improved during treatment, although progress was
uneven. That improvement does not alter the findings made at the earlier examination. Having read the clinical
record myself, I consider Dr Voss’s assessment well supported by the symptoms and observations she
documented.
I have confined this account to the medical findings relevant to your request; it is not intended as a complete
history of Ms Marlow’s care.
Yours sincerely,
Dr Rowan Pell
General Practitioner

notes: The professional status, video examination and clinical consistency judgement are supported. The different author’s access to the medical records is ambiguous. However, receiving a summary and describing the notes does not clearly establish whether the author had access to the applicant’s medical records. Basis: Schedule 1(11), guidance 2.52–2.60 and checklist, pp.18–21.

Alder Quay Surgery
9 July 2026
Dear Mr Cresswell,
Re: Nerys Bellan
I am writing with Ms Bellan’s permission concerning her consultation at this surgery on 21 May 2026. I am a
general practitioner, registered with the General Medical Council and licensed to practise, and held that status at
the time of her attendance.
The consultation was a clinical examination by video with Dr Mira Hesk, another GMC-registered and licensed
GP. Dr Hesk was registered and licensed when she examined Ms Bellan. She is now on leave and unavailable to
write personally.
A summary passed to me following the consultation describes recurrent panic episodes, interrupted sleep and
marked apprehension. Dr Hesk wrote the consultation notes. The assessment recorded there was that Ms Bellan
had an anxiety condition whose presentation was consistent with her having been a victim of domestic abuse.
This was Dr Hesk’s clinical judgement following the examination, rather than solely Ms Bellan’s explanation of her
symptoms.
Ms Bellan has since arranged a follow-up appointment to discuss treatment and the effect of the symptoms on her
working day. This letter concerns the findings at the May consultation and does not attempt to predict how long
her symptoms will continue.
Yours sincerely,
Dr Jonas Vale
General Practitioner

notes: The letter confirms an examination and an insomnia assessment, but gives only the patient’s attribution to domestic abuse, not the clinician’s consistency judgement. GP4 (missing): A condition is identified, but the only connection to domestic abuse is the patient’s belief. The clinician does not express a professional judgement that the condition is consistent with domestic abuse. Basis: Schedule 1(11), guidance 2.52–2.60 and checklist, pp.18–21.
text:
Willowglass Medical Practice
16 June 2026
Dear Ms Linton,
Re: Orla Daven
Orla asked me for a letter after our appointment last Thursday, 11 June. I examined her in person that afternoon. I
am her GP and am registered with the General Medical Council with a current licence to practise; I also held
registration and a licence at the appointment.
She has been having a difficult time with sleep, often waking very early and then feeling exhausted by lunchtime.
During the consultation I assessed persistent insomnia, with fatigue and some loss of concentration. We talked
through her evening routine, caffeine intake and the practical difficulty of resting when she has an early shift the
next morning.
Orla believes that domestic abuse during her previous relationship explains the sleep problem. She told me that
she still finds herself going over conversations from that period when the house is quiet. She wanted that part of
her account included here, as she feels it is easily lost when appointments focus on sleep advice.
We agreed on a short sleep diary and a further appointment in three weeks. I suggested that she bring the diary
even if it has gaps; it need not become another task to worry about.
With best wishes,
Dr Celia Norrick
General Practitioner

Merewick House Surgery
12 September 2026
Dear Sir or Madam,
Re: Mrs Ada Wrenfold
At Mrs Wrenfold’s request, I confirm that I examined her in person at this surgery on 7 February 2024. I was then,
and remain, a medical practitioner registered with the General Medical Council and licensed to practise as a
general practitioner.
At that examination she was suffering from an anxiety condition, with poor sleep, episodes of panic and difficulty
managing ordinary daily activities. My clinical judgement was that the condition identified at the consultation was
consistent with her having been a victim of domestic abuse. This assessment took account of both the history
obtained and her presentation during the examination.
She attended for several subsequent appointments and recieved treatment. By the autumn of 2024 her symptoms
had substantially improved. I mention this to distinguish her condition at the original examination from her later
progress.
The above account is drawn from my examination and the contemporaneous notes I made. Mrs Wrenfold has
consented to its release.
Yours faithfully,
Dr Edwin Sallow
General Practitioner

From: Isla Fenwick <isla.fenwick@rowanharbour.example>
To: Family Team <family@brackenfoldlaw.example>
Date: 18 September 2026
Subject: Support provided to Mairi Cresswell
Dear Family Team,
Mairi Cresswell has asked me to write about her contact with Rowan Harbour Support. We are a domestic abuse
support organisation based in Scotland, United Kingdom, and have operated continuously since February 2014. I
am Mairi’s allocated support worker and have met with her five times since June.
Mairi described how her former partner expected her to account for each journey outside the house, repeatedly
checked her messages and accused her of being disloyal when she spoke to friends. Since separation, she has
received repeated demands to explain where she is and who is with her. During one appointment, she showed me
a series of messages demanding photographs to prove her whereabouts. She had stopped attending an evening
class because she feared the response afterwards.
Taking these conversations and the messages together, my professional judgement is that Mairi has experienced
psychological domestic abuse and remains at risk of further controlling behaviour from her former partner.
We have worked through a safety plan, changed the privacy settings on her accounts together and helped her
identify a safe way to keep important documents. I also supported her to reconnect with a trusted friend and
accompanied her to a housing advice appointment.
She needed this support because the monitoring had left her isolated and unsure how to make ordinary decisions
safely. Our work has focused on restoring practical choices without increasing that risk. She continues to attend
fortnightly appointments.
Kind regards,
Isla Fenwick
Domestic Abuse Support Worker
Rowan Harbour Support

Celyn Bridge Domestic Abuse Support
Wales, United Kingdom
22 July 2026
Dear Ms Aldercombe,
I am writing at the request of Elin Marrick, whom I have supported since April. Celyn Bridge began its domestic
abuse work in Wales in 2013. There was a temporary closure during building repairs in 2021, before we reopened
at our present premises the following spring.
Elin first came to us after leaving the home she shared with her husband. She described being required to hand
over her wages, having to ask for money for bus fares and being challenged over small purchases. In our
appointments she showed me messages in which he demanded receipts and threatened to cancel her access to
their account. She also brought bank statements showing that her wages went into an account she could no
longer access independently.
In my professional judgement, Elin has been subjected to domestic abuse involving financial control and
intimidation. That view rests on our detailed discussions and the material she shared, rather than simply the fact
that she sought help.
I helped Elin prepare a safe budget, supported her through opening an account in her own name and arranged
food vouchers when she had no money available. We also completed a safety plan for collecting essential
belongings.
She needed this assistance because she lacked access to everyday funds and was frightened that taking steps
towards independence would lead to further threats. These were immediate difficulties, not merely concerns about
future expenditure.
Yours sincerely,
Bethan Veylock
Senior Support Practitioner

notes: All applicable requirements are supported. The newer outreach service and author's recent appointment do not undermine the organisation's confirmed continuity. Basis: Schedule 1(17), guidance 2.74–2.77 and checklist, pp.25–26.

Alderwake Domestic Abuse Partnership
England, United Kingdom
1 October 2026
Dear Sir or Madam,
Re: Daniel Norcombe
Alderwake Domestic Abuse Partnership has operated without interruption in England since May 2019. Our
neighbourhood outreach service opened on 1 August 2026. I joined the organisation in September and have
personally held three support appointments with Daniel Norcombe through that service.
Daniel sought help concerning his former civil partner. In reaching my professional judgement, I have relied
particularly on the following:
• Daniel’s account of being repeatedly prevented from sleeping by demands that he answer questions about
supposed infidelity.
• Messages he showed me threatening to disclose private information to his employer unless he returned home.
• His description of abandoning visits to his sister because each visit prompted prolonged accusations and
demands for access to his phone.
Considered together, these matters demonstrate a pattern of coercive and psychological domestic abuse. In my
reasonable professional judgement, Daniel has experienced that abuse and remains at risk of it continuing after
separation.
The support I have already provided includes:
• Developing a safety plan covering unwanted visits and safe communication.
• Helping Daniel secure his email account and remove shared access to his calendar.
• Accompanying him to a housing appointment and helping him organise documents for that meeting.
Daniel needed this help because the threats made him fearful of seeking accommodation independently, while
shared account access exposed his appointments and movements. He was also struggling to identify which
communications required a response. Our sessions have given him practical ways to reduce those risks while
maintaining necessary arrangements.
Yours faithfully,
Rory Penhalwick
Outreach Support Worker

notes: The letter supports the abuse judgement, its specific basis and completed support, but omits confirmation of at least six months' uninterrupted organisational operation. Merehaven Domestic Abuse Centre
England, United Kingdom
14 August 2026
Dear Ms Wrenholt,
Re: Nadia Bellmere
I write with Nadia Bellmere’s consent to confirm the support she has received from Merehaven Domestic Abuse
Centre. We are based in England and provide specialist domestic abuse advocacy and practical support. I am the
caseworker responsible for her support.
Across four appointments, Nadia described her husband taking her house keys during disagreements, preventing
her from attending appointments and threatening to remove her belongings if she stayed with relatives. She
showed me messages telling her she would be locked out if she did not return immediately. During our second
meeting, she explained that she had missed a housing appointment because she could not leave the property with
a key.
In my professional judgement, Nadia is experiencing domestic abuse through intimidation and control of her
movements and access to her home.
I have completed a safety plan with her, helped her arrange secure storage for copies of essential documents and
accompanied her to a rescheduled housing appointment. We have also agreed a safe method for our service to
contact her.
Nadia required this support because she feared losing access to her home and belongings, and the restrictions
were obstructing her attempts to obtain independent advice. Our assistance addressed those practical barriers
while taking account of her safety.
Yours sincerely,
Serena Ashcombe
Domestic Abuse Caseworker

Bracken Lantern Domestic Abuse Service
York, England, United Kingdom
18 September 2026
Dear Sir or Madam,
I am writing at the request of Mr Ellis Norcombe, whom I have supported since June. Ellis initially found it difficult
to describe his experiences as abuse because there had been no physical assault. That did not lessen the effect
on his everyday life.
During our appointments he explained that his former cohabiting partner, Rowan Pellin, required him to send
photographs showing where he was and repeatedly contacted his workplace when he did not answer immediately.
I have seen messages demanding those photographs and threatening to tell his employer private information
about him. Ellis also described abandoning visits to his sister because he expected prolonged questioning
afterwards. These accounts were consistent across our meetings.
We have worked together on a practical safety plan, including safer arrangements for collecting belongings. I
helped Ellis review his phone's location-sharing settings and accompanied him to an appointment with an
independent housing adviser. He needed this assistance because he was still sharing digital accounts with
Rowan, was uncertain how to leave those arrangements safely and had nowhere settled to stay after leaving their
home.
Bracken Lantern provides specialist domestic abuse support from our base in York, in the United Kingdom. The
organisation has operated continuously, without interruption, since February 2021.
Having assessed Ellis's account alongside the messages he showed me, my professional judgement is that he
has experienced domestic abuse through monitoring, intimidation and control by his former partner. Our support
remains available while he establishes independent arrangements.
Yours faithfully,
Merrin Dovale
Domestic Abuse Support Practitioner

Dear Ms Brell,

The Partnership is based in Cardiff, Wales, United Kingdom, and provides specialist support to people

Nessa was referred to us in July 2026 and has attended individual appointments during August and September.
My assessment draws on the referral information, her testimony during those appointments and subsequent case
discussions with our safeguarding lead. Having considered that material together, it is my reasonable professional

We have provided individual emotional support, completed a personal safety plan with her and helped her identify
suitable sources of housing and welfare advice. With her permission, I also arranged an appointment with an
independent advice service and supported her preparation for that appointment.
This assistance was needed because Nessa was distressed, unsure how to assess her current safety and finding

she considers her next steps. She remains on my active caseload.
Yours sincerely,
Celia Varn
Senior Domestic Abuse Practitioner
Alder Quay Support Partnership

Mosslark Family Safety Centre
Bristol, England, United Kingdom
9 September 2026
Dear Ms Trenn,
Thank you for asking me to write about Iona Bellwick. I am her allocated domestic abuse worker at Mosslark. We
are a specialist domestic abuse support organisation based in Bristol, in the United Kingdom, and have been
operating continuously since April 2022.
Iona described her former partner waiting outside her workplace twice after she had asked him not to contact her.
She showed me messages saying that he would keep turning up until she agreed to meet. One included a
photograph of the staff entrance. Her account and those messages form the basis of my professional opinion that
she is at risk of domestic abuse from her former partner.
Our work with Iona centres on safety planning and housing advocacy. The safety plan is to cover her journey
home, a trusted contact and what to do if he appears again. On the advocacy side, I would liaise with her housing
officer about safer access arrangements and keeping her new address confidential. These are the practical
priorities in her current support plan.
Iona needs this help because she is worried about being approached alone and is unsure which housing
arrangements can be changed. She has been particulary concerned about leaving work after dark.
Best wishes,
Tamsin Orvel
Domestic Abuse Worker

Sablebridge Safety Project
Sheffield, England, United Kingdom
30 September 2026
To whom it may concern,
Re: Mara Vennick
Sablebridge Safety Project provides domestic abuse support in Sheffield, England, United Kingdom. The
organisation began operating on 30 January 2026 and has operated continuously, without interruption, for eight
months.
Mara Vennick attended our service on 7 and 14 September. She sought help following threats from her former
partner, Tobin Ruskell, with whom she previously lived.
I read messages in which he said he would come to her new home, force his way inside and make her regret
leaving. A further message referred to the street where she now lives, although she had not given him that
address. Mara explained that she had changed her usual route home because she feared being followed.
In my reasonable professional judgement, Mara is at risk of domestic abuse from her former partner. She reported
no physical injury; my assessment rests on the threats, his apparent knowledge of her location and the
circumstances she described.
We completed a safety plan, agreed a check-in arrangement with a trusted friend and helped Mara secure her
online accounts. With her consent, I contacted her landlord to request a review of entrance security.
She needed this practical support because her address appeared to have been discovered and she did not know
how to reduce the resulting risks while remaining in her accommodation.
Yours faithfully,
Jalen Mervet
Service Coordinator
